question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The bank will grant the loan (a)/ provided that you (b)/ will submit all the documents (c)/ on time. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A condition clause introduced by "provided that", "if" or "unless" takes the simple present for a future action, and "will" is not used in it. So "will submit" must be "submit".

◦ Corrected sentence: The bank will grant the loan provided that you submit all the documents on time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The bank will grant the loan" is proper, with "will grant" in the main clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "provided that you" is proper, with "provided that" introducing a condition.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "on time." is proper, because "on time" means "punctually" and takes no article.

 

NOTE

 

• provided that he pays, if she comes, unless they apply (simple present in the condition), and not provided that he will pay.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

She prefers reading novels (a)/ than watching (b)/ television serials. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Prefer" is followed by "to" and not by "than" ("prefer A to B"), and both sides take the same form. So "than watching" must be "to watching".

◦ Corrected sentence: She prefers reading novels to watching television serials.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "She prefers reading novels" is proper, with "prefers" followed by a gerund.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "television serials." is proper, with "serials" as a plural noun.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "than" in part (b) is used after "prefers".

 

NOTE

 

• She prefers tea to coffee, He prefers walking to driving (prefer … to); She would rather walk than drive (would rather … than).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The scheme looks attractive on paper (a)/ and it has received (b)/ wide publicity, (c)/ so it has failed to reach the poor. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last idea is in contrast to the first two ("attractive" and "wide publicity" against "failed"), so a contrast conjunction is needed, and "so" (which shows result) is wrong. So "so it has failed" must be "but it has failed".

◦ Corrected sentence: The scheme looks attractive on paper and it has received wide publicity, but it has failed to reach the poor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The scheme looks attractive on paper" is proper, with "looks" followed by an adjective.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "and it has received" is proper, with "and" joining two similar ideas and the present perfect "has received".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "wide publicity," is proper, because "publicity" is an uncountable noun and takes no article.

 

NOTE

 

• It looks good, but it failed, She tried hard, yet she lost (contrast: but / yet), and not It looks good, so it failed.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If Rohit prefers cricket (a)/ and plays for hours every day, (b)/ his sister enjoys chess (c)/ and spends her evenings reading. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "While" or "whereas" is used to show a contrast between two facts, while "if" shows a condition. So "If Rohit prefers" must be "While Rohit prefers".

◦ Corrected sentence: While Rohit prefers cricket and plays for hours every day, his sister enjoys chess and spends her evenings reading.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "and plays for hours every day," is proper, with "plays" agreeing with "Rohit" and "for" used before a period of time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "his sister enjoys chess" is proper, with the singular verb "enjoys" agreeing with "sister".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and spends her evenings reading." is proper, with "spends … reading" and "her" agreeing with "sister".

 

NOTE

 

• While he likes tea, she likes coffee, The north is dry, whereas the south is wet (while / whereas for contrast).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Ritu is extremely talented (a)/ at painting, (b)/ and she lacks the confidence (c)/ to exhibit her work. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second idea ("lacks the confidence") is in contrast to the first ("extremely talented"), so "but" is needed and "and" is wrong. So "and she lacks the confidence" must be "but she lacks the confidence".

◦ Corrected sentence: Ritu is extremely talented at painting, but she lacks the confidence to exhibit her work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Ritu is extremely talented" is proper, with the adverb "extremely" modifying "talented".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "at painting," is proper, with "talented at" followed by a gerund.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "to exhibit her work." is proper, with "confidence to" followed by a base verb.

 

NOTE

 

• He is rich but unhappy, She is clever but lazy (but for contrast), and not He is rich and unhappy in a contrasting sense.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The audience remained silent (a)/ during the speaker was narrating (b)/ the tragic story. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "During" is a preposition followed by a noun, while "while" is a conjunction followed by a clause. So "during the speaker was narrating" must be "while the speaker was narrating".

◦ Corrected sentence: The audience remained silent while the speaker was narrating the tragic story.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The audience remained silent" is proper, with "remained" followed by an adjective.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the tragic story." is proper, because "narrate" is a transitive verb and takes a direct object.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "during" in part (b) is followed by a clause.

 

NOTE

 

• during the lecture, during the night (during + noun); while the teacher was speaking (while + clause).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The mother told the child (a)/ to hold her hand (b)/ in the crowded market (c)/ lest he will get lost. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Lest" (= for fear that) is followed by "should + base verb", or by the base form, and "will" is not used. So "lest he will get lost" must be "lest he should get lost".

◦ Corrected sentence: The mother told the child to hold her hand in the crowded market lest he should get lost.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The mother told the child" is proper, with "told" followed by an object.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "to hold her hand" is proper, with "told … to" followed by a base verb.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "in the crowded market" is proper, with "in" used before a place.

 

NOTE

 

• Walk carefully lest you should fall, Work hard lest you fail (lest + should / base verb), and not lest you will fall.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Prices of essential goods are higher then (a)/ what they were (b)/ two years ago. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Than" is used to compare two things after a comparative degree, while "then" is an adverb of time. So "higher then" must be "higher than".

◦ Corrected sentence: Prices of essential goods are higher than what they were two years ago.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "what they were" is proper, with "what" used as a relative pronoun for the earlier prices.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "two years ago." is proper, with "ago" used with the past.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "then" in part (a) is used in a comparison instead of "than".

 

NOTE

 

• taller than, more useful than (comparative + than); We met then, Finish this, then go (then = at that time / next).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

With both engines failing, (a)/ the pilot (b)/ had no choice than to land (c)/ the plane in a nearby field. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No choice" and "no alternative" are followed by "but" (= except) with a to-infinitive, and not by "than". So "no choice than to land" must be "no choice but to land".

◦ Corrected sentence: With both engines failing, the pilot had no choice but to land the plane in a nearby field.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "With both engines failing," is proper, with "with" followed by a noun and a present participle.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the pilot" is proper, as a singular subject that agrees with "had".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "the plane in a nearby field." is proper, with "land" followed by an object and "in" used before a field.

 

NOTE

 

• had no choice but to wait, had no option but to leave (no choice / option / alternative + but + to-infinitive).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The staff will (a)/ inform the passengers (b)/ well in advance (c)/ in case of the train is delayed. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In case of" is followed by a noun ("in case of delay"), while "in case" alone is followed by a clause. So "in case of the train is delayed" must be "in case the train is delayed".

◦ Corrected sentence: The staff will inform the passengers well in advance in case the train is delayed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The staff will" is proper, with the collective noun "staff" and "will" showing the future.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "inform the passengers" is proper, with "inform" followed by a direct object.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "well in advance" is proper, with "well" strengthening "in advance".

 

NOTE

 

• in case it rains (in case + clause); in case of rain, in case of emergency (in case of + noun).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The report leaves (a)/ no doubt whether the new (b)/ policy will help small farmers. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After a negative expression such as "no doubt", "that" is used, while "whether / if" is used after a positive doubt ("I doubt whether …"). So "no doubt whether" must be "no doubt that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The report leaves no doubt that the new policy will help small farmers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The report leaves" is proper, with the singular verb "leaves" agreeing with "report".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "policy will help small farmers." is proper, with "will help" followed by an object.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "whether" in part (b) is used after the negative "no doubt".

 

NOTE

 

• There is no doubt that he is honest; I doubt whether he is honest (no doubt + that; doubt + whether / if).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Her latest film is not as popular like her debut film was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as popular as.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a comparison of equality, the pattern is "as … as" (or "not so … as" in the negative), and the second half is always completed by "as", and not by "like" or "than". So "as popular like" must be "as popular as".

◦ Corrected sentence: Her latest film is not as popular as her debut film was.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "so popular like" — "so … as" can be used in the negative, but "like" cannot complete the comparison before a clause.

 

• Option 3: "as popular than" — "than" is used only after a comparative degree, and it does not follow "as popular".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "like" cannot complete the comparison "as popular".

 

NOTE

 

• as tall as, not as costly as (as … as); taller than, less costly than (comparative + than).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Scarcely had the bell rung than the children ran out of the classroom.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. when.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Scarcely" and "hardly" are followed by "when" (or "before"), and "than" is used with "no sooner". So "than" must be "when".

◦ Corrected sentence: Scarcely had the bell rung when the children ran out of the classroom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "then" — "then" is an adverb of time and cannot join the two clauses after "scarcely".

 

• Option 2: "that" — "that" is not the linking word after "scarcely".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "than" does not go with "scarcely".

 

NOTE

 

• Scarcely had he sat down when the phone rang; No sooner had he sat down than the phone rang.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Such was the aroma of the freshly baked bread that customers queued up outside the bakery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. The pattern "Such + be + noun + that + clause" is used for emphasis and shows a result, so "Such was the aroma … that customers queued up" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: Such was the aroma of the freshly baked bread that customers queued up outside the bakery.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "So was" — "so" is used before an adjective or adverb, and it cannot be followed by "was" and a noun in this pattern.

 

• Option 2: "Such as was" — "such as" introduces examples and does not show a result with "that".

 

• Option 3: "Much was" — "much" cannot be used in this pattern to show a degree that leads to a result.

 

NOTE

 

• Such was his anger that he left the room; So great was his anger that he left the room (Such / So great + be + subject + that).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The rope was so strong to hold the weight of two men.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. strong enough to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Adjective + enough + to + verb" shows that something is sufficient for a purpose. "So strong to" is wrong, because "so" needs a "that" clause, so it must be "strong enough to".

◦ Corrected sentence: The rope was strong enough to hold the weight of two men.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "too strong to" — "too … to" shows that something is not possible, and it would make the rope unable to hold the weight.

 

• Option 3: "so strong that to" — "so … that" is followed by a full clause, and not by "to".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "so … to" is not a correct pattern.

 

NOTE

 

• strong enough to lift, old enough to vote (adjective + enough + to); so strong that it did not break (so + adjective + that + clause).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The flight was cancelled due to the pilots had declared a strike.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. because.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Due to", "owing to" and "because of" are followed by a noun or noun phrase, while "because" is a conjunction followed by a clause. "The pilots had declared a strike" is a clause, so "due to" must be "because".

◦ Corrected sentence: The flight was cancelled because the pilots had declared a strike.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "in spite of" — this is a preposition showing contrast, and it does not give the reason.

 

• Option 2: "owing to" — this is a preposition and it cannot be followed by a full clause.

 

• Option 3: "because of" — this is a preposition and it cannot be followed by a full clause.

 

NOTE

 

• because he was late (because + clause); because of his delay, due to the strike, owing to the rain (preposition + noun).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Submit the form before 5 p.m., however it will not be accepted.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. otherwise.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Otherwise" (= if not) shows the result of not following an instruction, here "if you do not submit the form before 5 p.m.". "However" cannot join two clauses with a comma and does not give this meaning. So "however" must be "otherwise".

◦ Corrected sentence: Submit the form before 5 p.m., otherwise it will not be accepted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "moreover" — this adds one more point, and it does not show the result of not submitting the form.

 

• Option 3: "therefore" — this shows a result of something already done, and it does not give a warning.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "however" does not give the meaning "if not" and cannot join the two clauses.

 

NOTE

 

• Hurry up, otherwise you will miss the train, Work hard, otherwise you will fail (otherwise = if not).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The company will refund the full amount unless the product is returned undamaged within seven days.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. provided that.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Unless" means "if not" and reverses the meaning here. The refund is given only on the condition that the product is returned, so "provided that" is needed. So "unless" must be "provided that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The company will refund the full amount provided that the product is returned undamaged within seven days.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "although" — this shows contrast, and there is no contrast between the refund and the return of the product.

 

• Option 2: "until" — this shows the time up to which something happens, and it does not give a condition.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "unless" would mean that the refund is given if the product is not returned.

 

NOTE

 

• I will help you provided that you work, She will go provided that it does not rain (provided that = on condition that); unless = if … not.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Meera attended the rehearsal even she was running a high fever.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. even though.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Even" alone cannot join two clauses. The conjunction "even though" (= in spite of the fact that) is used to show a surprising contrast. So "even" must be "even though".

◦ Corrected sentence: Meera attended the rehearsal even though she was running a high fever.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "even so" — this means "nevertheless" and is an adverb, so it cannot join two clauses.

 

• Option 3: "even that" — this is not used as a conjunction to show contrast.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "even" alone cannot join two clauses.

 

NOTE

 

• He went out even though it was raining, She smiled even though she was hurt (even though + clause).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The trekkers will not reach the base camp before dark unless they start by dawn.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Unless" (= if … not) gives the condition for reaching the camp before dark, so "will not reach … unless they start by dawn" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: The trekkers will not reach the base camp before dark unless they start by dawn.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "until" — this shows the time up to which something continues, and it does not give a condition here.

 

• Option 2: "although" — this shows contrast, and the two ideas are not contrasting.

 

• Option 3: "because" — this gives a reason, and the start by dawn is a condition and not a reason.

 

NOTE

 

• You will not pass unless you study, She will not come unless he invites her (unless = if … not).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The volunteers reached the venue at dawn so that to arrange the stage before the crowd arrived.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. so as to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So as to" and "in order to" are followed by a base verb and show purpose, while "so that" and "in order that" are followed by a clause. So "so that to arrange" must be "so as to arrange".

◦ Corrected sentence: The volunteers reached the venue at dawn so as to arrange the stage before the crowd arrived.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "for to" — this is an old and incorrect form, and it is not used in standard English before a verb.

 

• Option 2: "in order that to" — "in order that" is followed by a clause and cannot be followed by "to".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "so that" is not followed by "to".

 

NOTE

 

• so as to save time, in order to save time (+ base verb); so that he could save time (+ clause).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Rohit would rather stay at home than to join the noisy party.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. than join.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pattern is "would rather + base verb + than + base verb", so "to" is not used after "than". So "than to join" must be "than join".

◦ Corrected sentence: Rohit would rather stay at home than join the noisy party.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "than joining" — the second verb must be in the same form as the first (base verb), and "joining" is a gerund.

 

• Option 3: "to join" — "rather" is completed by "than", and not by "to".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "than to join" adds "to" after "would rather … than".

 

NOTE

 

• I would rather walk than take a taxi, She would rather stay than go (would rather + base verb + than + base verb).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The northern plains are fertile even the deserts of the west receive very little rain.
option_1: so that the deserts of the west
option_2: whereas the deserts of the west
option_3: unless the deserts of the west
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whereas the deserts of the west.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Whereas" and "while" join two clauses that contrast with each other. Here the fertile plains are contrasted with the dry deserts, and "even" cannot join two clauses. So "even" must be "whereas".

◦ Corrected sentence: The northern plains are fertile whereas the deserts of the west receive very little rain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "so that the deserts of the west" — "so that" shows purpose or result, and it does not give a contrast.

 

• Option 3: "unless the deserts of the west" — "unless" gives a condition, and it does not give a contrast.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "even" cannot join the two clauses.

 

NOTE

 

• The north is cold, whereas the south is warm, Some people like tea, while others prefer coffee (whereas / while for contrast).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

No sooner you submit the form, you will get a receipt.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. As soon as you submit.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner", "hardly" and "scarcely" need the past perfect with inversion and are followed by "than / when" for a completed past event. For a present or future time clause, "As soon as" is used. So "No sooner you submit" must be "As soon as you submit".

◦ Corrected sentence: As soon as you submit the form, you will get a receipt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Hardly you submit" — "hardly" needs the past perfect with inversion and "when", and it cannot be used like this in a present time clause.

 

• Option 2: "Scarcely you submit" — "scarcely" needs the past perfect with inversion and "when", and it cannot be used like this in a present time clause.

 

• Option 3: "Just then you submit" — "just then" is an adverb meaning "at that moment", and it cannot introduce a time clause.

 

NOTE

 

• As soon as he arrives, I will call you, As soon as it stops raining, we will leave (as soon as + simple present, will in the main clause).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

I will lend you my notes as long as you return them by Friday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "As long as" (= provided that) introduces a condition, so "as long as you return them by Friday" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: I will lend you my notes as long as you return them by Friday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "as much as" — this shows quantity or degree, and it does not give a condition.

 

• Option 2: "so long that" — "so … that" shows a result, and it is not a condition.

 

• Option 3: "as far to" — this is not a correct conjunction, because "as far as" is the fixed form.

 

NOTE

 

• as long as you work hard, so long as you pay (as long as / so long as = provided that).
